title: Fuel Station Inspector
summary: Repair the discharge path from a charged worker to the Earth before they touch a fuel nozzle and strike a spark.
subject: physics
learningOutcome: After winning, the student can tell conductors from insulators, find the one break that stops a discharge path, choose between routes, and trade off resistance against cost.

levels.title: Ground the worker
levels.adds: Baseline: one lead from the worker to the Earth. Choose a material that lets the charge drain away.
hints: A charge can only flow through a material that has charges free to move.
Metals are conductors. Glass, plastic, rubber, nylon, porcelain and dry wood are insulators.
An insulator holds the charge where it is, so the worker stays charged and sparks at the nozzle.

levels.title: Find the break
levels.adds: New idea: the path has four parts in series, and one is an insulator. You may swap only one part, so find the one that breaks the path.
hints: In a path of parts one after another, the charge has to pass through every part.
A single insulator anywhere stops the whole path, however good the other parts are.
Swapping a part that already conducts changes nothing. Find the insulator and replace that one.

levels.title: Two ways out
levels.adds: New idea: two parallel routes to the Earth, each with insulators. Charge only needs one complete route, and you may swap just one part.
hints: Charge takes any route that is complete. You only need one to work.
Count the insulators on each route. Each one needs a swap.
With one swap you can only repair the route that has a single insulator.

levels.title: Dissipate it
levels.adds: Harder: parts have a resistance and a cost. A high-resistance path drains too slowly and still sparks. Stay under both limits.
hints: Resistances in series add up. Add the three you choose.
Semiconductors and salt-water gel conduct, but with more resistance than a metal. Insulators do not conduct at all.
You need the total resistance at or below the limit and the total cost within the cap. Try the cheapest option that still drains in time.

misconceptions: A metal object cannot hold a charge (it can, if it is insulated from the ground)
One good conductor in a chain is enough (every part must conduct)
Semiconductors and insulators behave the same
